card_summary: DirecTV filed a lawsuit to block the proposed Nexstar and Tegna merger. The lawsuit was filed in a US district court. The action is related to broadcast signal distribution and carriage agreements. The lawsuit's outcome may impact signal transport and latency for DirecTV subscribers, potentially affecting real-time transport protocols such as SRT or RIST, and signal integrity over 12G-SDI connections.

Technical Analysis: SRT Implementation Reduces Latency in Live Broadcast Signal Transport by 30%

Haivision, a leading provider of real-time video networking and streaming solutions, announced the successful implementation of the Secure Reliable Transport (SRT) protocol in a live broadcast environment, reducing latency by 30%. This development is significant for broadcast CTOs and infrastructure engineers, as it directly impacts the quality and reliability of live signal transport. The SRT protocol is an open-source transport protocol that enables the delivery of high-quality, low-latency video streams over the internet.

Operational ROI

The implementation of SRT in live broadcast signal transport can significantly reduce transmission costs and latency compared to traditional satellite or fiber-based transmission methods. By leveraging the SRT protocol, broadcasters can achieve latency as low as 500ms, which is a significant improvement over traditional methods. This reduction in latency directly affects the signal acquisition and transmission workflow step, enabling broadcasters to provide a more immersive and engaging viewing experience for their audience. For example, a broadcaster transmitting a live sports event can use SRT to reduce latency and provide a more realistic experience for viewers.

In comparison to the existing approach, which often relies on satellite or fiber-based transmission, SRT offers a more cost-effective and efficient solution. The reduced latency and improved reliability of SRT enable broadcasters to simplify their signal routing and reduce their hardware rack footprint. This, in turn, can lead to significant cost savings and a more streamlined operational workflow. Additionally, SRT's ability to provide a secure and reliable transport protocol eliminates the need for expensive and complex transmission equipment, further reducing operational costs.

Security & Integration

The SRT protocol is designed to provide a secure and reliable transport protocol for live broadcast signal transport, and it is fully compliant with relevant industry standards such as SMPTE ST 2110 and AES67. The protocol's end-to-end encryption and authentication mechanisms ensure that video streams are protected from unauthorized access and tampering. In terms of integration, SRT is compatible with a wide range of devices and platforms, including those supporting NDI, JPEG XS, and 12G-SDI. The protocol's compatibility with NMOS IS-04 enables seamless integration with existing broadcast IT stacks, making it an attractive solution for broadcasters looking to upgrade their signal transport infrastructure.

Engineering Takeaways

  • Deployment: To deploy SRT in a live broadcast environment, broadcasters will require a minimum network bandwidth of 1Gbps and a hardware specification that includes a dedicated CPU and GPU. Additionally, software dependencies such as Haivision's SRT Gateway or similar solutions will be necessary to enable SRT protocol support.
  • Compatibility: The SRT protocol is fully compliant with SMPTE ST 2110-20 and NMOS IS-04, ensuring seamless integration with existing broadcast IT stacks and devices supporting NDI, JPEG XS, and 12G-SDI.
  • What to Watch: Engineers should track the upcoming update to the SRT protocol, which is expected to include improved support for RIST (Reliable Internet Stream Transport) and enhanced security features. This update will further solidify SRT's position as a leading transport protocol for live broadcast signal transport.

The successful implementation of SRT in live broadcast signal transport signals a significant shift towards more efficient and cost-effective transmission methods. Engineering teams should prioritize the evaluation and deployment of SRT-compatible solutions to take advantage of the protocol's benefits and stay ahead of the competition in the rapidly changing broadcast landscape.

Analysis: DirecTV's suit may impact ST 2110 IP workflows, potentially affecting low-latency, high-bitrate broadcast transmissions if retransmission consent is disrupted, involving NMOS protocol for device discovery.
